title: The Einstein field equations
one_line_summary: Argues its way to G + Lambda g = kT by demanding a frame-free, second-order generalization of Poisson's equation that respects local energy-momentum conservation, introduces geometrized units, counts the true degrees of freedom, linearizes the equations around flat spacetime (gauge freedom, trace reversal, Lorentz gauge, box h-bar = -16 pi T), and uses the result to recover the Newtonian metric, fix k = 8 pi, and define the mass of any stationary body from its far field.
role_in_book: Chapters 5-7 built the geometry (curvature, Bianchi identities, Einstein tensor) and the kinematics of free fall in a given metric, including the weak-field metric of Eq. 7.8 that reproduces Newtonian orbits. This chapter closes the loop by supplying the dynamical law that tells matter how to curve spacetime. Its second half, linearized theory in the Lorentz gauge, is the working toolkit that Chapter 9 immediately reuses for gravitational waves, and its operational definition of mass and far-field metric (Eq. 8.60) set up the stellar and black-hole solutions of Chapters 10-11. Lambda is deliberately parked here and resurrected in Chapter 13.

assumed_background.topic: Stress-energy tensor of a fluid, MCRF energy density rho, and its symmetry (10 independent components)
Local conservation law T^{alpha beta}_{;beta} = 0 as a consequence of the equivalence principle
Riemann and Ricci tensors, Ricci scalar, Einstein tensor and the contracted Bianchi identity G^{alpha beta}_{;beta} = 0
Covariant differentiation and metric compatibility g^{alpha beta}_{;mu} = 0
Weak-field metric ds^2 = -(1+2 phi) dt^2 + (1-2 phi) dl^2 and its Newtonian geodesics (Kepler's laws)
Lorentz transformation matrices, the Minkowski metric eta, index raising and lowering, units with c = 1
Tensor transformation law under general coordinate changes (Lambda matrices as Jacobians)
Newtonian gravity: Poisson's equation, point-mass potential, Gauss's law, Kepler's third law
Electromagnetic potentials, gauge transformations and the Lorenz gauge in four-vector form
Wave equation and Laplace equation; multipole falloff of solutions of Laplace's equation
Taylor expansion to first order and geometric (Neumann) series for matrix inverses

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why neither the rest-frame energy density rho nor the single component T^{00} can be the source of a relativistic gravitational field, and why the whole stress-energy tensor must be.

Reader can list the requirements (second-order in the metric, symmetric (2 0) tensor, no preferred coordinates, conservation for every metric) that lead to the three-term family of Eq. 8.4 (Ricci tensor, a multiple of the metric times the Ricci scalar, and a multiple of the metric), and show that the contracted Bianchi identity forces mu = -1/2.

Reader can convert masses, densities, pressures, luminosities and accelerations between SI and geometrized units using G/c^2 and c^5/G, and explain why geometrized masses of the Earth and Sun are known far more precisely than their masses in kilograms.

Reader can count the independent content of Einstein's equations: ten equations, four Bianchi identities, four coordinate functions, six physical metric functions, and identify G_{0 alpha} = 8 pi T_{0 alpha} as constraint equations.

Reader can define a nearly-Lorentz coordinate system and distinguish the two coordinate changes that preserve it: background Lorentz transformations (under which h transforms like an SR tensor) and infinitesimal gauge transformations (h -> h - xi_{alpha,beta} - xi_{beta,alpha}).
Reader can write the linearized Riemann tensor and argue both algebraically and by an order-of-magnitude argument that it is gauge invariant.
Reader can define the trace-reversed perturbation h-bar, prove that trace reversal is its own inverse, and write the linearized Einstein tensor in terms of h-bar.

Reader can show that the Lorentz (harmonic, de Donder) gauge can always be reached by solving a wave equation for xi, explain the residual gauge freedom, and derive the linearized field equations box h-bar^{mu nu} = -16 pi T^{mu nu}.

Reader can carry out the Newtonian limit: justify the ordering |T^{00}| >> |T^{0i}| >> |T^{ij}|, reduce box to nabla^2 for slow sources, identify h-bar^{00} = -4 phi, and reconstruct the full metric of Eq. 8.50 including its spatial part, thereby confirming k = 8 pi.

Reader can explain why the Newtonian-limit metric cannot simply be applied outside a strongly gravitating source, and instead derive the far field of a stationary isolated source from the vacuum linearized equations plus the gauge condition.

Reader can define the total mass of a relativistic stationary body operationally from Keplerian orbits of distant test bodies, write the far-field metric Eq. 8.60, and state when the definition is and is not safe for time-dependent sources.
Reader can describe, at the level of the exercises, two post-Newtonian effects: the influence of a source's rotation (h-bar^{0j}) on orbital periods and the active gravitational mass rho + 3p.
Reader can explain why Lambda is set to zero for solar-system physics yet kept in principle, and estimate a solar-system bound on |Lambda|.

teaching_approach.summary: Schutz does not 'derive' Einstein's equations; he narrows the space of acceptable laws with a short chain of physical requirements borrowed from Newtonian gravity, relativity and the equivalence principle, then openly admits the result is a well-motivated guess that experiment has vindicated. The constant k is set to 8 pi provisionally and checked later. The linearized half of the chapter is a careful exercise in epistemic honesty about coordinates: the author repeatedly names 'convenient fictions' (h as a tensor on flat space), explains which transformations preserve them, slows down to read a non-tensorial component equation in words, and uses the electromagnetic gauge analogy to domesticate gauge freedom. Heavy algebra (linearized Riemann and Einstein tensors, trace-reversal identities, Lorentz gauge change) is asserted as 'easy to show' and delegated to a tightly scaffolded exercise set. The chapter ends with a physically important move: mass is defined by how a body is weighed, not by integrating over its interior.
narrative_arc: Motivating question: Chapters 5-7 say how matter moves in a curved metric; what law tells sources how to shape the metric? Newton's Poisson equation is the template.
Choose the source by eliminating preferred observers: rest-frame rho is rejected, then T^{00} is rejected, leaving the full tensor T and a proposed law O(g) = kT.
Constrain the operator: a symmetric (2 0) tensor built from g and its first and second derivatives, giving the family R + mu g R + Lambda g.
Impose conservation of T for every metric; compare with the contracted Bianchi identity to fix mu = -1/2 and arrive at G + Lambda g = kT.
Step back: other theories satisfy the same requirements; aesthetic economy and experimental tests favour Einstein's; quantum gravity may eventually require corrections.
Install geometrized units (G = c = 1) with Table 8.1 and a metrology argument about the Earth's mass.
Specialize to Lambda = 0 and k = 8 pi as a promise to be verified; recount the equations as six independent ones because of Bianchi identities and coordinate freedom; point to numerical relativity.
Define weak fields through the existence of nearly-Lorentz coordinates and defend choosing convenient coordinates.

Identify two transformation classes that preserve weak-field form: background Lorentz transformations (h behaves like an SR tensor, the flat-background fiction) and small gauge transformations (h shifts by symmetrized derivatives of xi).
Linearize curvature: Riemann to first order and its gauge invariance; raise indices with eta; introduce the trace reverse; state the linearized Einstein tensor.
Simplify with the Lorentz gauge, prove it can be reached by solving a wave equation, note residual freedom, and obtain box h-bar = -16 pi T.
Check against Newton: component ordering for slow sources, box -> nabla^2, h-bar^{00} = -4 phi, reconstruct Eq. 7.8 and thereby confirm k = 8 pi.
Look beyond Newton: post-Newtonian effects, solar-system tests, the Hulse-Taylor pulsar and gravitational-wave observations.

Apply linearized theory where it is legitimate, far from a possibly strong stationary source: solve Laplace's equation, use the gauge condition to kill all but h-bar^{00}, define the far-field potential and then the total mass via orbits, giving Eq. 8.60.
Qualify the mass definition for time-dependent sources and hand post-Newtonian extensions (rotation, pressure as active mass, Lambda bounds) to the exercises.
signature_moves: Elimination-by-invariance: candidate sources are tried in order of increasing sophistication and each is discarded because it would single out a class of observers.
Deferred calibration: set k = 8 pi at the outset for later convenience, promise verification, and later make the reader redo the limit with arbitrary k (Exercise 8.16).
Counting functions against identities: four Bianchi identities matched with four free coordinate functions to explain why only six of the ten equations carry physics.
Explicitly labelled fictions: treating h as a tensor on a flat background is flagged as a useful fiction valid only under background Lorentz transformations.
Reading an equation aloud: the author translates the 0-0 component of Eq. 8.22 into a full English sentence to teach how primed indices and non-tensorial relations work.
Metrology as motivation for units: the nine-figure precision of GM for the Earth versus the four-figure precision of G shows that geometrized mass is the natural observable.
Operational definitions over integrals: the mass of a relativistic body is whatever Kepler's law infers from distant orbits.
Heavy delegation to scaffolded exercises: the text says 'one can show' and supplies step-by-step exercises (8.5, 8.7, 8.8, 8.10, 8.12, 8.14) for the algebra.
Borrowing electromagnetism's vocabulary (gauge, Lorentz gauge, wave operator) and making the analogy precise in Exercise 8.11.

sections.title: Purpose and justification of the field equations
sections.summary: Starts from Poisson's equation as the Newtonian law linking source to potential and asks for its relativistic replacement. The source must be observer-independent, so the full stress-energy tensor replaces mass density, and the metric replaces the potential. A second-order tensor operator on the metric must equal kT; the admissible family is Ricci plus multiples of g R and g. Requiring that the equations imply conservation of T for any geometry, and using the contracted Bianchi identity, selects the Einstein tensor and yields G + Lambda g = kT with two constants still free. The section then acknowledges that the three requirements do not single out Einstein's theory, mentions competing theories and precision tests, quotes Chandrasekhar's stance on aesthetic criteria, and notes that quantum gravity may eventually modify the theory.
concepts: stress-energy tensor as the source of gravity
requirements on the gravitational field operator
key_moves: Reject rho (tied to the MCRF) and T^{00} (tied to a chosen frame) as sources; adopt the whole tensor T, giving ten equations O(g) = kT.

Demand O^{alpha beta} be a (2 0) tensor built from g_{mu nu}, g_{mu nu,lambda}, g_{mu nu,lambda sigma}; propose the Ricci tensor plus constant multiples of (metric x scalar curvature) and of the metric itself (Eq. 8.4).
Since T^{alpha beta}_{;beta} = 0 for every metric, O^{alpha beta}_{;beta} must vanish identically; with g^{alpha beta}_{;mu} = 0 this requires (R^{alpha beta} + mu g^{alpha beta} R)_{;beta} = 0.
Compare with Eq. 6.98 to get mu = -1/2, giving G^{alpha beta} + Lambda g^{alpha beta} = k T^{alpha beta}.
Summarize the three criteria and concede non-uniqueness; justify ignoring alternatives on simplicity and experimental grounds.

sections.title: Geometrized units (subsection of 8.1)
sections.summary: Before fixing k the author sets G = 1 as well as c = 1, using the conversion factor G/c^2 to express masses in metres. Table 8.1 lists SI and geometrized values of c, G, hbar, electron and proton masses, solar and terrestrial masses and the solar luminosity. A metrological aside explains that orbit tracking measures GM, so geometrized masses of the Earth and Sun are known to about nine figures while their kilogram values inherit the roughly 1e-4 uncertainty in laboratory G.
key_moves: Extend the SR habit of c = 1 to G = 1 for gravitational problems.
Use 1 = G/c^2 = 7.425e-28 m/kg to eliminate kilograms.
Argue that geometrized mass is the directly measured quantity in orbital dynamics, so it is more precise than SI mass.

sections.title: Einstein's equations
sections.summary: Sets Lambda = 0 and k = 8 pi to obtain G^{alpha beta} = 8 pi T^{alpha beta}, with a short history of the cosmological constant (introduced for a static universe, abandoned after the expansion was discovered, now observationally favoured as small but nonzero; deferred to Chapter 13 and Exercise 8.18). Explains that k = 8 pi is fixed by the Newtonian limit and will be verified. Interprets the equations as ten coupled nonlinear PDEs for the metric with a well-posed initial-value problem, then shows why they cannot determine all ten metric components: four coordinate functions are arbitrary, matched by the four Bianchi identities, so only six equations constrain the six geometric functions. Numerical relativity is named as the field that separates gauge from physics in practice.
concepts: coordinate freedom and counting of degrees of freedom
key_moves: Specialize Eq. 8.7 to Lambda = 0, k = 8 pi and flag both choices as provisional.
Count: symmetric G and T give ten equations for ten g_{alpha beta}.
Coordinate changes involve four arbitrary functions, so initial data cannot fix all ten components to the future.
Bianchi identities G^{alpha beta}_{;beta} = 0 supply four differential relations, leaving six independent equations for six geometric functions.

sections.title: Einstein's equations for weak gravitational fields
sections.summary: Defines a weak field as a spacetime admitting coordinates in which g = eta + h with all |h| small, stressing 'there exist' because even flat spacetime has coordinates far from eta. Defends choosing convenient coordinates even though physics is coordinate-free, with the examples of free motion in polar coordinates and non-separable Poisson problems. Introduces background Lorentz transformations, with constant Lorentz matrices, under which h transforms exactly like a tensor in special relativity, which licenses the fiction of h as a field on flat spacetime. Introduces small gauge transformations x' = x + xi, derives h -> h - xi_{alpha,beta} - xi_{beta,alpha} to first order, names it by analogy with electromagnetism, and pauses to explain how to read the non-tensorial Eq. 8.22 component by component.
concepts: valid tensor equation versus component relation
key_moves: Define weak fields by existence of coordinates with |h_{alpha beta}| << 1.
Transform g = eta + h with a constant Lorentz matrix: eta is invariant, so h picks up exactly the SR tensor transformation (Eq. 8.19).
For x' = x + xi with |xi^alpha_{,beta}| << 1, write the Jacobian and its inverse to first order (Eqs. 8.20-8.21) and transform g to get Eq. 8.22.
Interpret the result as a change of h alone (Eq. 8.24), which keeps the coordinates nearly Lorentz if xi's derivatives are small.
Explain that primes mark the coordinate system, not different index values, and that Eq. 8.22 relates components in two specific systems rather than being a tensor equation.

sections.title: Linearized curvature, trace reversal and the Lorentz gauge (continuation of 8.3)
sections.summary: States the first-order Riemann tensor in terms of second derivatives of h and explains its gauge invariance: a coordinate change mixes curvature components linearly, and a small change applied to already-small components is second order. Adopts the flat-background viewpoint consistently, treats gauge transformations as equivalence relations rather than coordinate changes, raises indices with eta, and defines the trace h and the trace-reversed h-bar, whose inverse relation has the same form. Gives the linearized Einstein tensor in terms of h-bar, observes that it simplifies if the divergence of h-bar vanishes, and proves this Lorentz gauge is always attainable: the divergence changes by box xi under a gauge transformation, so one solves an inhomogeneous wave equation for xi. Any solution of the homogeneous wave equation can be added, so the Lorentz gauge is a family. In this gauge G = -(1/2) box h-bar and the linearized field equations are box h-bar = -16 pi T.
concepts: index raising with the background metric
key_moves: Linearize R_{alpha beta mu nu} (Eq. 8.25) and argue gauge invariance by an order-counting argument (proof in Exercise 8.5).
Declare gauge transformations to define equivalence classes of h, keeping all equations as SR tensor equations.
Define h^{mu nu}, h and h-bar; show h-bar's trace is -h and the inverse map is identical (Exercise 8.7).
Write G_{alpha beta} in terms of h-bar (Eq. 8.32; derivation scaffolded in Exercise 8.8).
Count four gauge conditions against four gauge functions; show h-bar divergence shifts by -box xi^mu (Eqs. 8.34-8.35) and solve box xi^mu = old divergence.
Note non-uniqueness (add any eta^mu with box eta^mu = 0), then reduce G to -(1/2) box h-bar and obtain Eq. 8.42.

sections.title: Newtonian gravitational fields
sections.summary: Under the Newtonian subsection, the author assumes |phi| << 1 and v << 1, argues that stress-energy components are ordered |T^{00}| >> |T^{0i}| >> |T^{ij}| (with caveats for spherical stars and rotating stars) and that this ordering carries over to h-bar when no gravitational waves are present. The dominant equation is box h-bar^{00} = -16 pi rho; for slowly moving sources time derivatives are down by v, so box becomes nabla^2. Matching to Poisson's equation gives h-bar^{00} = -4 phi; trace reversal then yields h^{00} = h^{xx} = h^{yy} = h^{zz} = -2 phi, i.e. exactly the metric of Eq. 7.8. Since that metric reproduces Newton's laws of motion, Newtonian gravity is shown to be a limit of GR and k = 8 pi is confirmed.
key_moves: State the Newtonian regime as weak field plus slow motion.
Order T components by powers of v, transfer the ordering to h-bar via Eq. 8.42, excluding homogeneous (wave) solutions.
Keep only box h-bar^{00} = -16 pi rho with T^{00} = rho + O(rho v^2).
Use d/dt ~ v d/dx to replace box by nabla^2.
Match to nabla^2 phi = 4 pi rho: h-bar^{00} = -4 phi.
Compute h = h-bar^{00}, then h^{00} and h^{ii} = -2 phi, giving ds^2 = -(1+2 phi)dt^2 + (1-2 phi)dl^2 and confirming k.

sections.title: Post-Newtonian corrections and observational tests (within 8.4)
sections.summary: A short survey: most astronomical systems are Newtonian to first approximation but post-Newtonian corrections matter for precision tests such as Mercury's perihelion advance and solar light deflection (Chapter 11), and for the orbital decay of the Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar (Chapter 9). Gravitational-wave detections of inspiralling and merging compact binaries test both high-order post-Newtonian orbits and full numerical simulations, and allow comparison of the speeds of gravitational and electromagnetic waves (Chapter 12). Post-Newtonian theory is developed to very high order.
key_moves: Place the Newtonian limit as the leading term of a systematic expansion.
List solar-system, pulsar and gravitational-wave tests as applications of corrections beyond that leading term.

sections.title: The far field of stationary relativistic sources (within 8.4)
sections.summary: Considers an isolated source that may have strong internal gravity. Far away spacetime is asymptotically flat and linearized theory applies, but the Newtonian-limit result cannot be carried over, because its derivation assumed weak gravity inside the source and because no Newtonian potential exists for a strongly relativistic body. Instead, for a stationary source the vacuum linearized equations reduce to Laplace's equation for each h-bar component, with 1/r leading solutions A^{mu nu}/r. The Lorentz gauge condition, applied at all angles, forces A^{mu j} = 0, so only h-bar^{00} survives at order 1/r. This justifies defining a far-field 'Newtonian potential' as -h-bar^{00}/4, after which Eq. 8.50 describes the far field.
concepts: far field of a stationary source
multipole falloff of solutions of Laplace's equation
key_moves: Explain two reasons the Newtonian-limit metric is not automatically the far field of a relativistic body.
Use stationarity to reduce Eq. 8.42 in vacuum to nabla^2 h-bar^{mu nu} = 0 with solution A^{mu nu}/r + O(r^-2).
Impose the gauge condition: -A^{mu j} n_j / r^2 must vanish for all directions n, so A^{mu j} = 0.
Conclude h-bar^{00} dominates and define phi_far = -h-bar^{00}/4 by reversing Eq. 8.46.

sections.title: Definition of the mass of a relativistic body (within 8.4)
sections.summary: Renames A^{00} as 4M so the far-field potential is -M/r. Distant test bodies then follow Keplerian orbits for mass M, so M is defined as the total mass of the source: it is inferred from orbits, exactly as astronomers weigh planets and stars, not by summing constituent masses. The far-field metric of any stationary source is written with 1 -/+ 2M/r factors (Eq. 8.60). The author warns that M may differ from naive Newtonian expectations (pressure contributes; Exercise 8.20), and explains when the definition still works for time-dependent sources: when waves are weak compared with the stationary field, or when the source was stationary in the past and one measures beyond the wave front.
concepts: total mass of a stationary relativistic body
far field of a stationary source
key_moves: Match the far-field phi to the Newtonian -M/r by setting A^{00} = 4M.
Invoke Chapter 7: geodesics of Eq. 8.50 obey Kepler's laws, so M is the Keplerian mass.
Define total mass operationally (weighing by orbits) and write Eq. 8.60.
Discuss limits of validity for sources that radiate.

sections.title: Bibliography
sections.summary: Points to alternative justifications of the field equations, to rigorous geometric (Cartan) and asymptotic treatments of the Newtonian limit, to post-Newtonian reviews, and to historical scholarship on Einstein's notebooks. Offers a graded list of GR textbooks from introductory to demanding, and recommends a problem book as a supplement.
key_moves: Admit that the chapter's Newtonian limit was heuristic and point to rigorous treatments.
Grade the textbook literature by required background.

sections.title: Exercises
sections.summary: Twenty exercises: point-mass potential via Gauss's law; unit conversion and Planck scales; potentials and orbital speeds in geometrized units; matrix inverse series; gauge invariance of linearized Riemann; inverse metric perturbation; trace-reversal identities; a guided derivation of the linearized Einstein tensor; constraint versus evolution equations; reaching Eq. 8.41; the electromagnetic gauge analogy; the gauge change of h-bar; justifying the component ordering; completing and generalizing the Newtonian limit (arbitrary k, coordinate-free measurements); weighing a neutron star and a black hole from proper circumferences and periods; bounds on Lambda; the field of a rotating body and its effect on orbital periods; and active gravitational mass rho + 3p.
key_moves: Scaffold every 'one can show' step of the chapter with a dedicated exercise.
Extend the Newtonian limit to rotation and pressure as first post-Newtonian effects.

concepts.name: Poisson equation for Newtonian gravity
concepts.definition: The Newtonian field law nabla^2 phi = 4 pi G rho relating the gravitational potential to the mass density; for a point mass its decaying solution is phi = -Gm/r.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the template the relativistic law must generalize: a second-order differential operator on the field equals a constant times the source density. Its point-mass solution is left to Exercise 8.1 via Gauss's law.

concepts.name: stress-energy tensor as the source of gravity
concepts.definition: In a relativistic theory the whole symmetric stress-energy tensor T^{alpha beta}, not a single observer's energy density, generates the gravitational field, so energy density, momentum density and stresses all gravitate.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached by elimination: rest-frame energy density rho is frame-specific, T^{00} depends on the chosen frame, so only the full tensor avoids a preferred observer. Returns in Exercises 8.19-8.20 where momentum density and pressure produce measurable effects.

concepts.name: requirements on the gravitational field operator
concepts.definition: The conditions used to narrow the relativistic field law: it should generalize Poisson's equation (second order in derivatives of the metric, a symmetric (2 0) tensor equated to kT), introduce no preferred coordinates, and guarantee T^{alpha beta}_{;beta} = 0 for every metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Built step by step from the Newtonian analogue, then summarized as criteria (i)-(iii) with the explicit caveat that other equations also meet them.
concepts.notes: The text does not mention Lovelock's theorem, which is the rigorous statement that in four dimensions these criteria force the Einstein tensor plus a cosmological term.

concepts.name: Ricci tensor and Ricci scalar
concepts.definition: The contraction R_{alpha beta} = R^mu_{alpha mu beta} of the Riemann tensor and its trace R = g^{alpha beta} R_{alpha beta}; both involve the metric and its first and second derivatives.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 6 as the obvious symmetric (2 0) tensor built from second derivatives of g, the first ingredient of the candidate operator.

concepts.name: contracted Bianchi identity
concepts.definition: The geometric identity G^{alpha beta}_{;beta} = 0, which holds for any metric; it is the contracted form of the differential Bianchi identity for the Riemann tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Used twice: first to select mu = -1/2 so that the field equations are compatible with conservation for any metric, then to explain that the ten Einstein equations obey four identities and so contain only six independent equations.

concepts.name: local conservation of energy-momentum
concepts.definition: The statement T^{alpha beta}_{;beta} = 0, required by the Einstein equivalence principle; in a local inertial frame it reduces to special-relativistic energy and momentum conservation.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Eq. 7.6 as a property of T not yet exploited; because it must hold for any metric, it demands that the geometric side be identically divergence-free.

concepts.name: metric compatibility of the connection
aliases: vanishing covariant derivative of the metric
concepts.definition: For the Levi-Civita connection the covariant derivative of the metric vanishes, g_{alpha beta;mu} = 0 = g^{alpha beta}_{;mu}, so the metric factors pass through covariant derivatives.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked in one line to drop the divergence of the Lambda g term and to move g outside the divergence of mu g R.

concepts.name: Einstein tensor
concepts.definition: The symmetric tensor G^{alpha beta} = R^{alpha beta} - (1/2) g^{alpha beta} R, which is identically divergence-free and is the geometric side of Einstein's equations.
concepts.how_introduced: Emerges as the unique member of the family R + mu g R with vanishing divergence, by comparison with Eq. 6.98. Later linearized in terms of h-bar.

concepts.name: Einstein field equations
concepts.definition: The dynamical law of general relativity, G^{alpha beta} + Lambda g^{alpha beta} = 8 pi T^{alpha beta} (geometrized units), relating spacetime curvature to the stress-energy of matter; with Lambda = 0 it reads G = 8 pi T.
concepts.how_introduced: Arrived at as the simplest law satisfying the chapter's three criteria, first with unknown constants k and Lambda, then specialized to Lambda = 0 and k = 8 pi, with k verified in the Newtonian limit. Interpreted as ten coupled nonlinear PDEs for the metric.
prerequisites: stress-energy tensor as the source of gravity
requirements on the gravitational field operator
concepts.notes: The author calls the argument a justification rather than a derivation, and stresses non-uniqueness.

concepts.name: cosmological constant
concepts.definition: A constant Lambda multiplying g^{alpha beta} that may be added to the field equations without spoiling conservation; moved to the right side it acts like the stress-energy -Lambda g^{alpha beta}/(8 pi) of empty space.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears automatically in the most general admissible operator, is left undetermined by the Newtonian limit, given a brief history (static universe, later abandoned, now observationally favoured) and set to zero until Chapter 13; Exercise 8.18 bounds it from planetary orbits.

concepts.name: gravitational coupling constant k = 8 pi
concepts.definition: The constant multiplying T in Einstein's equations; its value 8 pi (8 pi G/c^4 in SI) is fixed by requiring that the weak, slow limit reproduce Poisson's equation with the correct 4 pi G.
concepts.how_introduced: Set to 8 pi at the start of §8.2 for convenience with a promise to verify it; confirmed at the end of the Newtonian-limit derivation, and Exercise 8.16 asks the reader to redo the limit with general k.

concepts.name: general covariance
concepts.definition: The requirement that physical laws be expressible as tensor equations valid in all coordinate systems, so no class of observers or coordinates is privileged.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the criterion that eliminates rho and T^{00} as sources and requires a tensorial operator; later balanced against the practical need to choose good coordinates.

concepts.name: alternative theories of gravity
concepts.definition: Theories other than GR that also give relativistic, generally covariant, conservation-respecting gravitational laws, often with extra fields; many have been ruled out by precision tests since the 1960s.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised to admit that the criteria do not single out Einstein's equations; dismissed on grounds of greater complexity and experimental success of GR, with references to Will.

concepts.name: quantum gravity
concepts.definition: A yet-unknown quantum theory of gravitation, expected to modify GR at some level, possibly via extra fields coupled to the metric that could violate the equivalence principle or add wave polarizations.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the reason to keep testing GR despite its success.

concepts.name: geometrized units
concepts.definition: A unit system with both c = 1 and G = 1, in which mass, time and energy are measured in metres, using 1 = G/c^2 = 7.425e-28 m/kg and 1 = c^5/G = 3.629e52 W.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by analogy with setting c = 1 in SR and by metrology: orbits measure GM, so geometrized masses are known far better than SI ones. Table 8.1 and Exercise 8.2 build fluency.

concepts.name: Planck length
concepts.definition: The length (hbar G/c^3)^{1/2} = 1.616e-35 m formed from c, G and hbar; together with the Planck mass and time it marks where quantum gravity is expected to matter.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears in Exercise 8.2(d) as the square root of hbar in geometrized units (Table 8.1 gives hbar = 2.612e-70 m^2).
concepts.notes: The printed exercise uses hbar throughout; the text export drops the bar and shows plain h, so do not treat that as a book typo.

concepts.name: initial-value formulation of general relativity
concepts.definition: The property that Einstein's equations, suitably gauge-fixed, determine the future geometry from appropriate initial data, although the coordinates to the future remain freely choosable.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated without proof while interpreting G = 8 pi T as ten coupled PDEs; immediately qualified by the coordinate-freedom count.
prerequisites: coordinate freedom and counting of degrees of freedom

concepts.name: coordinate freedom and counting of degrees of freedom
concepts.definition: Of the ten metric components, four can be changed arbitrarily by coordinate transformations; correspondingly the four contracted Bianchi identities make only six of the ten Einstein equations independent, constraining the six coordinate-independent metric functions.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued from the impossibility of predicting all ten g_{alpha beta} when future coordinates can be relabelled at will, then matched with the Bianchi identities.

concepts.name: constraint equations
concepts.definition: The four components G_{0 alpha} = 8 pi T_{0 alpha}, which contain no second time derivatives of the metric and so restrict the initial data rather than evolving it; the six G_{ij} equations are the dynamical ones.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in Exercise 8.9 by inspecting the linearized Einstein tensor, and linked back to the counting in §8.2.

concepts.name: numerical relativity
concepts.definition: The computational solution of the full Einstein equations for dynamical spacetimes, which requires separating coordinate (gauge) freedom from physical degrees of freedom.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the practical arena where the counting argument matters, with references; later tied to merger simulations compared with gravitational-wave data.

concepts.name: weak gravitational field
concepts.definition: A spacetime admitting coordinates in which the metric differs from the Minkowski form by small perturbations, |h_{alpha beta}| << 1, throughout the region of interest.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined as the natural first approximation to curved spacetime, with the caveat that the statement is about existence of such coordinates, not all coordinates.

concepts.name: nearly-Lorentz coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates in which g_{alpha beta} = eta_{alpha beta} + h_{alpha beta} with all |h_{alpha beta}| << 1; if one such system exists, infinitely many do (related by background Lorentz and gauge transformations).
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the smart coordinate choice for weak fields; the text stresses that even flat spacetime has coordinates that are not nearly Lorentz.

concepts.name: metric perturbation
concepts.definition: The small symmetric array h_{alpha beta} = g_{alpha beta} - eta_{alpha beta} in nearly-Lorentz coordinates, treated in linearized theory as a symmetric tensor field on flat spacetime defined up to gauge transformations.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in Eq. 8.12 and then given tensor-like status by the background Lorentz argument.

concepts.name: choice of convenient coordinates
concepts.definition: The practice of exploiting coordinate freedom to choose coordinates in which the equations and their physical interpretation are simplest, while recognizing that predictions are coordinate independent.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by a rhetorical question about why to specialize at all, answered with familiar examples (free motion in polar coordinates, non-separable Poisson problems) and the remark that building good coordinates is an art.

concepts.name: background Lorentz transformation
concepts.definition: A coordinate transformation x^{alpha-bar} = Lambda^{alpha-bar}_beta x^beta with a constant special-relativistic Lorentz matrix; applied to eta + h it leaves eta invariant and transforms h exactly as an SR tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as one of two transformation classes that preserve nearly-Lorentz form, via a direct transformation of Eq. 8.12.

concepts.name: flat-background picture of linearized gravity
aliases: h as a tensor in SR
concepts.definition: The viewpoint that a weakly curved spacetime can be treated as flat Minkowski spacetime carrying a symmetric tensor field h_{mu nu}, with all linearized quantities written as SR tensor equations; it is a bookkeeping device valid only under background Lorentz transformations, the spacetime being truly curved.
concepts.how_introduced: Named explicitly as a fiction right after showing that h transforms like an SR tensor under background Lorentz maps; adopted consistently when deriving the linearized equations.

concepts.name: gauge transformation in linearized gravity
concepts.definition: The change of h under a small coordinate shift x'^alpha = x^alpha + xi^alpha(x) with |xi^alpha_{,beta}| << 1: to first order h_{alpha beta} -> h_{alpha beta} - xi_{alpha,beta} - xi_{beta,alpha}, which leaves all physical (curvature) quantities unchanged.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the first-order Jacobian and its inverse, then named by analogy with electromagnetic gauge transformations (Exercise 8.11). Reinterpreted as an equivalence relation among h rather than a coordinate change.
concepts.notes: Sign convention: other books use x' = x - xi and get plus signs.

concepts.name: valid tensor equation versus component relation
concepts.definition: A tensor equation has matching free indices and holds in every coordinate system; a relation such as Eq. 8.22 connects components in two specific coordinate systems, need not have matching index decorations, and is not coordinate invariant.
concepts.how_introduced: Explained in an extended aside that reads the 0-0 component of Eq. 8.22 aloud, aimed at beginners confused by primes on indices.

concepts.name: linearized Riemann tensor
aliases: Riemann tensor to first order in h
concepts.definition: The curvature tensor of a nearly flat metric eta + h to first order in h, where products of Christoffel symbols drop out and each component is one half of an antisymmetrized combination of four second partial derivatives of h (Eq. 8.25).
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as easy to show from the Chapter 6 formula with Christoffel-squared terms dropped.

concepts.name: gauge invariance of linearized curvature
concepts.definition: The first-order Riemann components are unchanged by gauge transformations: substituting h = xi_{alpha,beta} + xi_{beta,alpha} into the linearized Riemann tensor gives zero, and physically a small coordinate change alters already-small curvature components only at second order.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as an order-of-magnitude argument in the text and proved algebraically in Exercise 8.5, which links it to Killing's equation (Exercise 7.10).

concepts.name: index raising with the background metric
concepts.definition: In linearized theory indices on h and on derivatives are raised and lowered with eta rather than g, consistent with treating h as an SR tensor; a caution follows: the doubly raised perturbation obtained this way equals minus, not plus, the first-order change of the inverse metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in Eqs. 8.26-8.27 and 8.23, with the inverse-metric subtlety left to Exercise 8.6.

concepts.name: inverse metric to first order
concepts.definition: If g_{mu nu} = eta_{mu nu} + h_{mu nu} then g^{mu nu} = eta^{mu nu} - h^{mu nu} + O(h^2), from the series (I + A)^{-1} = I - A + A^2 - ...
concepts.how_introduced: Exercises 8.4 and 8.6.

concepts.name: trace-reversed metric perturbation
concepts.definition: h-bar^{alpha beta} = h^{alpha beta} - (1/2) eta^{alpha beta} h, where h = h^alpha_alpha; its trace is -h and the same operation applied to h-bar returns h. The linearized field equations are simplest in terms of h-bar.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined with its name justified by the sign flip of the trace; its self-inverse property is left to Exercise 8.7. Exercise 8.8 shows the linearized Einstein tensor is itself the trace reverse of the linearized Ricci tensor.
prerequisites: index raising with the background metric

concepts.name: linearized Einstein tensor
aliases: G to first order in h
concepts.definition: The Einstein tensor of eta + h to first order, written in terms of the trace reverse as G_{alpha beta} = -(1/2)[h-bar_{alpha beta,mu}^{,mu} + eta_{alpha beta} h-bar_{mu nu}^{,mu nu} - h-bar_{alpha mu,beta}^{,mu} - h-bar_{beta mu,alpha}^{,mu}].
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as not difficult to obtain from the linearized Riemann tensor, with a guided derivation in Exercise 8.8.

concepts.name: Lorenz gauge in linearized gravity
concepts.definition: The gauge condition h-bar^{mu nu}_{,nu} = 0 (four conditions), which can always be imposed by a gauge transformation and reduces the linearized Einstein tensor to -(1/2) box h-bar.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the visible simplification of Eq. 8.32 and by counting four conditions against four gauge functions; existence proved by showing the divergence changes by -box xi and invoking solvability of the wave equation.
concepts.notes: The book spells it 'Lorentz gauge'; historically the electromagnetic condition is due to Ludvig Lorenz.

concepts.name: residual gauge freedom
concepts.definition: After reaching the Lorenz gauge, any further gauge vector satisfying the homogeneous wave equation box eta^mu = 0 preserves the gauge condition, so the Lorenz gauge is a family of gauges rather than a unique one.
concepts.how_introduced: Noted immediately after the existence proof; exploited in Chapter 9 to reach transverse-traceless form.

concepts.name: d'Alembertian
concepts.definition: The flat-spacetime wave operator box f = eta^{mu nu} f_{,mu nu} = (-d^2/dt^2 + nabla^2) f.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced while solving for the gauge vector; box f = g is identified as the inhomogeneous wave equation, solvable for well-behaved sources.

concepts.name: linearized Einstein field equations
concepts.definition: In the Lorenz gauge and to first order in h, Einstein's equations become ten decoupled flat-space wave equations box h-bar^{mu nu} = -16 pi T^{mu nu}.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by inserting the Lorenz gauge into the linearized Einstein tensor; the basis for the Newtonian limit, the far field, and the next chapter's gravitational waves.

concepts.name: electromagnetic gauge analogy
concepts.definition: The parallel between h -> h - xi_{alpha,beta} - xi_{beta,alpha} and A_alpha -> A_alpha + f_{,alpha}, and between the gravitational Lorenz gauge h-bar^{mu nu}_{,nu} = 0 and A^mu_{,mu} = 0; in both cases potentials carry redundancy that leaves fields unchanged.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to justify the words 'gauge' and 'Lorentz gauge' and developed in Exercise 8.11.

concepts.name: Newtonian limit of general relativity
concepts.definition: The regime |phi| << 1, v << 1 without significant gravitational radiation, in which the linearized Einstein equations reduce to Poisson's equation for h-bar^{00} = -4 phi and the metric becomes ds^2 = -(1+2 phi)dt^2 + (1-2 phi)(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2), reproducing Newtonian dynamics.
concepts.how_introduced: Carried out explicitly as the check that fixes k = 8 pi, using component ordering and quasi-static reduction; admitted in the bibliography to be heuristic.

concepts.name: slow-motion ordering of stress-energy components
concepts.definition: For sources with v << 1, typically |T^{00}| >> |T^{0i}| >> |T^{ij}| (energy density, then momentum density ~ rho v, then stresses ~ rho v^2 or p), an ordering that the linearized equations pass on to h-bar in the absence of waves.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted with caveats (non-rotating spherical stars have T^{0i} = 0; rapidly rotating ones have T^{0i} >> T^{ij}); Exercise 8.13 asks for physical justification.

concepts.name: quasi-static approximation box to Laplacian
concepts.definition: When fields change only because sources move at speed v, time derivatives are of order v times space derivatives, so box = nabla^2 + O(v^2 nabla^2) and the wave equation becomes Poisson's equation at lowest order.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as one line in the Newtonian limit.

concepts.name: weak-field metric
concepts.definition: The line element ds^2 = -(1+2 phi)dt^2 + (1-2 phi)(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2) with phi the Newtonian potential; its geodesics give Newton's laws, and far from any stationary source it takes the form with phi = -M/r.
concepts.how_introduced: Imported from Chapter 7 as an ansatz, now derived from Einstein's equations, and later generalized to the far field of relativistic sources (Eq. 8.60).

concepts.name: gravitational waves as homogeneous solutions
concepts.definition: Solutions of box h-bar^{mu nu} = 0 that are not tied to local sources; their amplitudes are not controlled by the ordering of T components and they propagate at the speed of light.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the exception to the component ordering and to the stationary mass definition; developed in Chapter 9.

concepts.name: post-Newtonian effects
concepts.definition: Corrections to Newtonian gravity of higher order in v^2 and phi, such as perihelion precession, light deflection, gravitomagnetic effects of rotating bodies and pressure contributions to active mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Surveyed after the Newtonian limit with solar-system and pulsar examples, and made concrete in Exercises 8.19-8.20.

concepts.name: binary pulsar tests
concepts.definition: Precision timing of binary pulsars, especially the Hulse-Taylor system, which shows orbital shrinkage matching GR's prediction for energy loss to gravitational radiation.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited as the most important post-Newtonian test outside the Solar System.

concepts.name: gravitational-wave tests of general relativity
concepts.definition: Tests using detected inspiral-and-merger signals of binary black holes and neutron stars, compared with post-Newtonian waveforms and numerical relativity, including bounds on the difference between gravitational and light speeds.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as a recent expansion of testing opportunities, forward-referenced to Chapter 12.

concepts.name: asymptotic flatness
concepts.definition: A spacetime whose curvature falls off at large distance from a localized source, so that far away it approaches Minkowski spacetime and linearized theory applies.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the setting for the far-field analysis of possibly strongly gravitating sources.

concepts.name: far field of a stationary source
concepts.definition: Far from any stationary isolated source, in Lorenz gauge, h-bar^{mu nu} = A^{mu nu}/r + O(r^-2) with the gauge condition forcing A^{mu j} = 0, so only h-bar^{00} = 4M/r survives at order 1/r and the metric is ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r)dt^2 + (1 + 2M/r)(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2) up to O(r^-2).
concepts.how_introduced: Derived directly from the vacuum linearized equations without assuming weak internal gravity, after explaining why the Newtonian-limit shortcut is illegitimate here.
prerequisites: multipole falloff of solutions of Laplace's equation

concepts.name: multipole falloff of solutions of Laplace's equation
concepts.definition: A solution of nabla^2 f = 0 that vanishes at infinity outside a bounded region behaves as a constant over r plus terms falling off faster (O(r^-2)).
concepts.how_introduced: Used without comment to write Eq. 8.52; Exercise 8.19 supplies the Green's-function integral.

concepts.name: total mass of a stationary relativistic body
aliases: gravitational mass from the far field
concepts.definition: The constant M appearing in the far-field potential -M/r of an isolated stationary source, equivalently the mass inferred from Kepler's third law for distant test orbits; it is defined by the exterior field, not by integrating over the interior.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined operationally by 'weighing' the source with distant orbits, as astronomers do for the Earth and Sun; caveats for radiating sources are discussed.
prerequisites: far field of a stationary source
concepts.notes: This is the linearized precursor of the ADM and Komar masses, which the text does not name.

concepts.name: active gravitational mass
concepts.definition: The effective source of the Newtonian-like potential in a stationary, weakly self-gravitating system with possibly large stresses: nabla^2 Phi = 4 pi (rho + T^k_k), which for a perfect fluid is rho + 3p.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in Exercise 8.20 by trace-reversing the linearized equations; referenced in §8.4 to warn that far-field mass need not match Newtonian expectations.

concepts.name: gravitomagnetism
aliases: frame dragging in the weak field
concepts.definition: The part of the weak gravitational field sourced by momentum density T^{0j}; for a rotating body h-bar^{0j} falls as 1/r^2 and is proportional to the angular momentum, so prograde and retrograde orbits have different periods.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears only in Exercise 8.19 as the first worked post-Newtonian effect, contrasted with Newtonian gravity where rotation does not affect the field.
prerequisites: stress-energy tensor as the source of gravity
concepts.notes: The book does not use the words gravitomagnetism or Lense-Thirring here.

key_equations.name: Newtonian field equation
key_equations.meaning: Poisson's equation: the Newtonian potential is sourced by mass density; the template for the relativistic law.
key_equations.symbols: phi Newtonian potential; rho mass density; G Newton's constant

key_equations.name: Point-mass potential
key_equations.meaning: Potential of a point mass, dimensionless when c = 1.

key_equations.name: Schematic relativistic field law
key_equations.meaning: A second-order differential operator on the metric equals a constant times the full stress-energy tensor; ten equations.
key_equations.symbols: O unknown operator; g metric; T stress-energy tensor; k constant

key_equations.name: Candidate operator
key_equations.meaning: General symmetric (2 0) tensor built from the metric and its first two derivatives considered by the text.
key_equations.symbols: R^{alpha beta} Ricci tensor; R Ricci scalar; mu, Lambda constants

key_equations.name: Local conservation (recalled Eq. 7.6)
key_equations.meaning: Energy-momentum conservation demanded by the equivalence principle for any metric.

key_equations.name: Divergence-free operator
key_equations.meaning: Consequence of Eq. 8.3 and conservation; must hold identically for every metric.

key_equations.name: Condition fixing mu
key_equations.meaning: After dropping the Lambda term via metric compatibility; comparison with the contracted Bianchi identity (6.98) forces mu = -1/2.

key_equations.name: Einstein field equations with Lambda
key_equations.meaning: The field equations of GR with cosmological constant Lambda and coupling k still undetermined.
key_equations.symbols: G^{alpha beta} Einstein tensor; Lambda cosmological constant

key_equations.name: Index-free field equations
key_equations.meaning: Same law in geometric notation.

key_equations.name: Geometrized conversion factor
key_equations.meaning: Converts kilograms to metres, defining geometrized units c = G = 1.

key_equations.name: Einstein's equations
key_equations.meaning: The field equations with Lambda = 0 and k = 8 pi (geometrized units); ten coupled nonlinear PDEs for the metric.

key_equations.name: Bianchi identities
key_equations.meaning: Four differential identities among the ten Einstein-tensor components, making only six field equations independent.

key_equations.name: Weak-field decomposition
key_equations.meaning: Metric in nearly-Lorentz coordinates as Minkowski plus perturbation.
key_equations.symbols: eta Minkowski metric diag(-1,1,1,1); h perturbation

key_equations.name: Weak-field condition
key_equations.meaning: All perturbation components small everywhere in the region.

key_equations.name: Lorentz boost matrix
key_equations.meaning: Standard boost along x recalled for background Lorentz transformations.

key_equations.name: Background Lorentz transformation
key_equations.meaning: Linear coordinate change with constant SR Lorentz matrix.

key_equations.name: Transforming the weak-field metric
key_equations.meaning: Metric transformation law split into background and perturbation parts.

key_equations.name: Invariance of eta
key_equations.meaning: Defining property of Lorentz transformations.

key_equations.name: Weak-field form preserved
key_equations.meaning: Background Lorentz transformations keep nearly-Lorentz form.

key_equations.name: h transforms like an SR tensor
key_equations.meaning: Under background Lorentz maps h behaves exactly as a (0 2) tensor in SR, the basis of the flat-background fiction.

key_equations.name: Infinitesimal coordinate change
key_equations.meaning: Small, position-dependent shift generating a gauge transformation.

key_equations.name: Jacobian of gauge change
key_equations.meaning: Transformation matrix for the small coordinate shift.

key_equations.name: Inverse Jacobian
key_equations.meaning: First-order inverse, justified by the matrix series of Exercise 8.4.

key_equations.name: Metric after gauge change
key_equations.meaning: Components in the new coordinates in terms of old-coordinate quantities; not a tensor equation.

key_equations.name: Lowering xi
key_equations.meaning: Index lowered with the background metric.

key_equations.name: Gauge transformation of h
key_equations.meaning: The effect of a small coordinate change is a symmetrized-gradient shift of the perturbation; physically equivalent h's differ by such terms.

key_equations.name: Linearized Riemann tensor
key_equations.meaning: Curvature to first order in h; gauge invariant.

key_equations.name: Index raising with eta
key_equations.meaning: Definitions consistent with treating h as an SR tensor.

key_equations.name: Trace of h
key_equations.meaning: Trace with respect to eta.

key_equations.name: Trace reverse
key_equations.meaning: Trace-reversed perturbation; the natural variable for the linearized equations.

key_equations.name: Trace flips sign
key_equations.meaning: Justifies the name; uses eta^alpha_alpha = 4.

key_equations.name: Trace reversal is an involution
key_equations.meaning: Applying trace reversal twice returns the original.

key_equations.name: Linearized Einstein tensor
key_equations.latex: G_{\alpha\beta} = -\tfrac12\left[\bar h_{\alpha\beta,\mu}{}^{,\mu} + \eta_{\alpha\beta}\bar h_{\mu\nu}{}^{,\mu\nu} - \bar h_{\alpha\mu,\beta}{}^{,\mu} - \bar h_{\beta\mu,\alpha}{}^{,\mu} + O(h^2_{\alpha\beta})\right]
key_equations.meaning: First-order Einstein tensor in terms of the trace reverse (derived in Exercise 8.8); the last three terms vanish in Lorenz gauge. Export garbled the comma-index placement; recovered from the rendered page.

key_equations.name: Raised derivative index
key_equations.meaning: Notation reminder for derivative indices raised with eta.

key_equations.name: Lorenz (Lorentz) gauge condition
key_equations.meaning: Four gauge conditions that simplify the linearized Einstein tensor; also called harmonic or de Donder gauge.

key_equations.name: Gauge change of h-bar
key_equations.meaning: Trace-reversed version of Eq. 8.24 (Exercise 8.12). The final divergence term was garbled in the export and is recovered from the rendered page.

key_equations.name: Change of the divergence
key_equations.meaning: Only the wave operator acting on xi survives in the divergence.

key_equations.name: Equation for the gauge vector
key_equations.meaning: Solving this inhomogeneous wave equation takes any h to Lorenz gauge.

key_equations.name: d'Alembertian
key_equations.meaning: Flat-space wave operator, also written Delta.

key_equations.name: Inhomogeneous wave equation
key_equations.meaning: Always solvable for sufficiently well-behaved g; the text calls it three-dimensional, meaning three space dimensions.

key_equations.name: Residual gauge vectors
key_equations.meaning: Any homogeneous wave solution can be added to xi without leaving Lorenz gauge. Note eta^mu here is a vector, not the metric.

key_equations.name: Non-uniqueness of Lorenz gauge
key_equations.meaning: Lorenz gauge is a class of gauges.

key_equations.name: Einstein tensor in Lorenz gauge
key_equations.meaning: Linearized Einstein tensor reduces to a wave operator (Exercise 8.10).

key_equations.name: Linearized field equations
key_equations.meaning: Weak-field Einstein equations in Lorenz gauge: decoupled wave equations sourced by stress-energy.

key_equations.name: Dominant Newtonian equation
key_equations.meaning: Only the 00 component matters for slow sources; uses T^{00} = rho + O(rho v^2).

key_equations.name: Quasi-static wave operator
key_equations.meaning: Time derivatives are suppressed by v for slowly moving sources.

key_equations.name: Poisson form
key_equations.meaning: Lowest-order Newtonian field equation for h-bar^{00}.

key_equations.name: Identification with the potential
key_equations.meaning: Matching with nabla^2 phi = 4 pi rho (G = 1).

key_equations.name: Trace in the Newtonian limit
key_equations.meaning: Only h-bar^{00} contributes, with eta_{00} = -1 flipping the sign.

key_equations.name: Time-time perturbation
key_equations.meaning: From trace reversal of h-bar^{00}.

key_equations.name: Spatial perturbations
key_equations.meaning: Spatial diagonal components are generated entirely by the trace term, even though h-bar^{ij} is negligible.

key_equations.name: Newtonian-limit metric
key_equations.meaning: Identical to Eq. 7.8; proves Newtonian gravity is a limit of GR and confirms k = 8 pi.

key_equations.name: Stationary vacuum far field
key_equations.meaning: Linearized equations outside a stationary source.

key_equations.name: Monopole falloff
key_equations.meaning: Leading far-field solution with constant A^{mu nu}.

key_equations.name: Gauge condition in the far field
key_equations.meaning: Time independence reduces the divergence to spatial derivatives.

key_equations.name: Unit radial normal
key_equations.meaning: Direction cosines of the field point.

key_equations.name: Vanishing of mixed and spatial monopoles
key_equations.meaning: Because n_j is arbitrary, all A with a spatial index vanish.

key_equations.name: Far-field dominance of h-bar^{00}
key_equations.meaning: Far field is Newtonian-like even for strongly gravitating sources.

key_equations.name: Definition of far-field potential
key_equations.latex: (\phi)_{\rm relativistic\ far\ field} := -\tfrac14(\bar h^{00})_{\rm far\ field}
key_equations.meaning: Reverses Eq. 8.46 as a definition.

key_equations.name: Newtonian far field
key_equations.meaning: Monopole potential of a Newtonian source.

key_equations.name: Relativistic far-field potential
key_equations.meaning: With A^{00} = 4M; M is then defined as total mass.

key_equations.name: Far-field metric of any stationary source
key_equations.meaning: Universal exterior weak field parametrized by the total mass. The printed equation shows 0(r^-2) with a zero where O is meant.

key_equations.name: Conversion for power (Exercise 8.2)
key_equations.meaning: Luminosities become dimensionless in geometrized units.

key_equations.name: Gauss-law step (Exercise 8.1)
key_equations.meaning: Radial field of a spherically symmetric point source, integrated with phi -> 0 at infinity to get Eq. 8.2.

key_equations.name: Matrix inverse series (Exercise 8.4)
key_equations.meaning: Justifies first-order inverses such as Eq. 8.21 and g^{mu nu} = eta^{mu nu} - h^{mu nu}.

key_equations.name: Inverse metric perturbation (Exercise 8.6)
key_equations.meaning: The raised-index h is minus the deviation of the inverse metric.

key_equations.name: Linearized Einstein tensor as trace reverse (Exercise 8.8)
key_equations.meaning: To first order the Einstein tensor is the trace reverse of the Ricci tensor.

key_equations.name: Circular orbit speed (Exercise 8.3f)
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian circular-orbit relation, used to show v^2 and |phi| are the same small parameter.

key_equations.name: Green's function for Poisson (Exercise 8.19)
key_equations.meaning: General decaying solution of nabla^2 f = g; used to solve for h-bar^{00} and h-bar^{0j} of a rotating body.

key_equations.name: Trace-reversed linearized equations
key_equations.meaning: Equivalent form of Eq. 8.42 sourced by the trace-reversed stress-energy.

key_equations.name: Active gravitational mass
key_equations.meaning: For weak internal gravity but strong stresses, the far-field potential is sourced by rho plus the spatial trace of T (rho + 3p for a perfect fluid).
